name: Map local pack rankings across a geo grid with Bright Data, GPT-5.6, Slack and Gmail

parameters.content:
## Map where you show up in the local pack, street by street

A local business does not have one ranking. It has a different one every few streets, because Google answers with whatever is near the person asking. This checks a grid of points around you and draws the result.

### How it works

**`Build The Grid`** turns a centre point and a spacing into a square of coordinates, and builds a `uule` for each one - the parameter that tells Google to answer as if the searcher were standing there. Verified live: three coordinates returned three completely different local packs, and repeating each point gave the same place back.

**`Loop Over The Grid`** walks the points one at a time, because every point is one SERP request and a burst earns a rate limit that arrives as HTTP 200.

**`Read The Local Pack`** finds your business in each pack and records the position, or records that you were not in it. **`Find Who Beats You`** then tallies the competitors sitting above you, across all the points where they did.

**`Draw The Map`** lays the ranks out in the shape of the ground, GPT-5.6 writes the two sentences a client will actually read, and the week is stored in a Data Table so next week can be compared to it.

### Setup

1. Bright Data: a SERP zone as one Header Auth credential. Free tier is 5,000 credits a month, no card.

2. An OpenAI credential, a Slack credential and a Gmail credential.

3. A Data Table called `local_grid` with columns `watch_key`, `business`, `keyword`, `run_on`, `coverage_pct`, `avg_rank` and `in_pack`.

4. In **Settings**: your business name as Google spells it, the search term, and the centre latitude and longitude. Start at `grid_size` 3.

## 1. A centre point becomes a square of coordinates
An odd grid size puts your own address in the middle square, which is the reference every other point is read against.

## 2. One point at a time
Each square is a search run as if the customer were standing there. Verified live: three coordinates returned three different local packs, twice each.

## 3. Score it, then compare it
If Google reported no location at any point the map is one search repeated, and the run stops rather than drawing conclusions from it.

## 4. Who is standing where you are not
The part a single rank cannot give you: a rival who beats you at two edge points is a different problem from one who beats you at nine.

## 5. Two sentences, not a dashboard
The model gets the drawn map and the rival tally, and is asked for the two lines an owner will actually read.

## 6. The team and the owner
Slack gets the map in a code block so the grid keeps its shape; the owner gets the same thing as HTML.

## This measures the pack, not a rank beyond it

The local pack is three results deep, occasionally four. A point where you do not appear tells you that you are not in the top three *there* - it does not tell you whether you are fourth or fortieth, and this workflow will never claim to know. Google's deeper local list does not come back in a form that can be parsed, so the honest measure is presence.

**Every point is a request, every week, forever.** A 3x3 grid is 9 a week; 5x5 is 25; 7x7 is 49. Raise `grid_size` only after you have seen what one run costs, and remember that a wider grid mostly adds points where no local business ranks anywhere.

Matching is on your business name as text. If Google lists you under a slightly different name - an old trading name, an extra suffix - you will read as absent everywhere. Check one point by hand before you believe a map of zeros.

Local results move on their own. A single week's change at one point is not a trend, and this is a map to look at over a month rather than a number to report on Monday.
